topic.topic: Normal distribution and the central limit theorem
topic.angle: Galton's bean machine as a bell-curve maker

body.claim: Averages of many independent random values form a bell curve, even when the individual values do not.
body.why: This is the central limit theorem: the distribution of a sample mean approaches the normal distribution, even if the original variables are not normally distributed. In Francis Galton's bean machine, beads bounce left or right off rows of pegs, and the piles in the bins at the bottom approximate a bell curve.

probes.question: What does the central limit theorem say about a sample mean?
options: It is always exactly the true mean
Its distribution approaches a normal distribution
It gets more skewed as the sample grows
It only works for bell-shaped data

probes.question: True or false: the individual values must themselves be normally distributed for the central limit theorem to apply.

claims.claim: Distribution of the sample mean approaches the normal distribution (central limit theorem)
claims.quote: the distribution of a normalized version of the sample mean converges to a standard normal distribution

claims.claim: This holds even if the original variables are not normally distributed (also probe false)
claims.quote: This holds even if the original variables themselves are not normally distributed .

claims.claim: Galton's bean machine: beads bounce left or right off rows of pegs
claims.quote: Beads are dropped from the top and, when the device is level, bounce either left or right as they hit the pegs

claims.claim: Piles in the bins approximate a bell curve
claims.quote: the height of bead columns accumulated in the bins approximate a bell curve

claims.claim: Bean machine invented by Francis Galton
claims.quote: is a device invented by Francis Galton to demonstrate the central limit theorem
